newsitem.title: UK: Britain, Ireland, to review vexed N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland, to review vexed N.Ireland.

text.p: Britain and Ireland hold their first 1997 ministerial-level talks on Northern Ireland on Wednesday against a background of mounting IRA guerrilla violence and deepening community mistrust.

Irish calls for a new British investigation into the 1972 Bloody Sunday slayings of 13 Catholic demonstrators and efforts to defuse tension surrounding the yearly Protestant marching season will dominate the Belfast discussions, officials said.
But few decisive measures on Northern Ireland are expected until Britain holds a general election, which is due by May, Irish officials said.

The Dublin government says it will collate new evidence about Bloody Sunday, when British paratroopers opened fire on a civil rights march in Londonderry killing 13 people, and give it to Britain in an attempt to secure a new investigation.

The Irish government's move follows the 25th anniversary of the Londonderry killings on January 30 and the publication of a book and other reports suggesting previously unreported British army sniper fire on the crowd.

An official investigation of the incident, which hardened Catholic attitudes towards Britain and helped the Irish Republican Army recruit more guerrillas, exonerated British sodliers who said they were returning fire.
But Catholics say the shooting was unprovoked and accuse the London authorites of a cover-up. Britain says it will only open a fresh inquiry if it receives new evidence.
Wednesday's meeting follows a huge demonstration by Catholics in Londonderry on Sunday and calls by Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, for an international public investigation.

The IRA has attacked police and army targets in Northern Ireland every few days this year in an apparent effort to force retaliation by their Protestant Loyalist foes, who are officially observing an October 1994 ceasefire.

Security analysts say the apparent aim of the IRA, which has yet to claim its first fatality of 1997, is to revisit the province with sectarian mayhem so that whatever government takes over after British elections due by May has to rebuild a moribund peace process.
Sinn Fein is banned from the Belfast peace talks until the IRA ends violence altogether and the negotiations are in limbo awaiting the election for fresh impetus.

IRA violence aimed at forcing a British withdrawal from Northern Ireland to reunite the province with the Irish republic has deepened sectarian tension since the guerrillas ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year, police said.

The Irish government is anxious that a lid is kept on such tension in the run-up to the start of the yearly marching season at the end of March and disappointed at Britain's reluctance to adopt in full an independent commission's recommendations.
The commission last month proposed that an independent body be given the power to ban marches, which only the police are currently empowered to do.

Last year Northern Ireland erupted into the worst civil unrest for more than a decade when police first banned but then allowed a Protestant Orange Order march to the tiny church of Drumcree on the outskirts of the southern town of Portadown.
The move allowed the Protestant order to parade through a Catholic section of Portadown, enraging members of the minority faith across the province and igniting fresh violence.
